comparator.name: Political Science: Global Politics
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from VU Amsterdam's current official sources for the Fall-2026 cohort: the Bachelor Political Science: Global Politics curriculum page, its future/career page, and the 2026-2027 Teaching and Examination Regulations (OER/TER) for the Bachelor's programme Political Science (RIO 56606), the formally adopted regulation governing the programme, offered by the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities. Article 10.2 confirms that, starting cohort 2025-2026, the programme offers exactly two named tracks -- 'Politicologie: Nationale Politiek en Bestuur' (Dutch) and 'Political Science: Global Politics' (English) -- so the normalized target itself names this exact official route; Article 10.1 confirms its specifically global orientation (graduates prepared for international, supranational, transnational and global levels) and Article 10.4.1 confirms English as its language of instruction. Article 10.3's Global Politics learning outcomes name international conflict and cooperation, international security, global political economy, societal/technological developments, normative political theory, and general/comparative politics and International Relations as the programme's defining content. Year 1 (Article 11.1 Academic core plus Article 11.3 major; Appendix III 'BACHELOR POLITICAL SCIENCE 2026-2027, English-language track, New Curriculum from cohort 2025-2026 onwards', 60 EC, all compulsory): Comparative Politics, Democracies and Other Regimes (S_CPDO), The Governance and Politics of Social Problems (S_GPSP), History of Political Thought (S_HPT), Political Analysis of Current Challenges (S_PACC), Academic Skills Workshop Political Science 1 and 2 (S_ASWPS1/2), International Relations: Conflict and Cooperation (S_IRCC), Social Research Methodology (S_SRM), Descriptive and Inferential Statistics (S_DIS), History of Social Sciences (S_HSS). Year 2 (Appendix III, same table, 60 EC): Global Governance (S_GG), The European Union in the Global Order (S_EUGO), Qualitative Research and Methods in Political Science (S_QLRMPS), International Security (S_ISPS), Research Project Global Politics 1: Quantitative Methods and 2: Qualitative Research (S_RPGP1/2), Quantitative Research and Methods in Political Science (S_QRMP), Global Political Economy (S_GPE) are compulsory; Article 12 and Appendix III additionally require two restricted-choice 'Social Science for Society' electives shared with Sociology/Communication Science students, each offered as one of three period-specific options -- no target-specific evidence favours one option over the others offered in either period slot, so the first-listed option in the OER's own Appendix III timetable is used as the neutral tie-break in each slot (Beyond Gender Inequalities for the period-4 slot; AI & Society: Fixing Algorithmic Decision Making for the period-5 slot). Year 3: Article 12.1 fixes the first semester as at least 30 EC of elective units of education -- a minor, an individually chosen package (at least 12 EC at level 300), or an approved internship -- with no single content fixed by the OER, preserved as open space; the current official curriculum page confirms the second semester's capstone as Philosophy of Science, Contemporary Political Theory and the Graduation Project Global Politics for the current (Fall-2026) cohort. The OER's own Appendix III prints this Year-3 structure only under its 'Old Curriculum (cohort 2024/2025 or before)' table -- Philosophy of Science (S_PS, 6 EC), Contemporary Political Theory (S_CPT, 6 EC), Bachelor's Thesis Project Global Politics (S_BTPGP, 18 EC) -- because the first New-Curriculum cohort (2025-2026) will not reach Year 3 until 2027-2028, one edition beyond this OER; the current official curriculum webpage independently confirms the identical structure, name and codes apply to the Fall-2026 cohort, so the two current official sources jointly and consistently establish it. Article 9.1 requires at least 90 EC from the programme (excluding electives), including Academic Skills Workshop Political Science 1 and 2, before the Bachelor's Thesis Project Global Politics may be taken. 60 (Year 1) + 60 (Year 2) + 60 (Year 3) = 180 EC. No further official source needed to be consulted: the curriculum page, future page and OER together establish a complete, internally consistent, entirely accounted-for 180-EC pathway with explicit EC weights and compulsory/elective status for every component, and explicit, UCR-independent elective-tie-break judgments fixed before any UCR course was considered.

alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to the Global Politics target: a broad, generalist political-science programme that reproduces as closely as UCR's catalogue allows the comparator's own compulsory breadth -- comparative politics and regimes, International Relations theory, the EU's role in the global order, global political economy, international law and governance, security and conflict, the historical and cultural causes of political change, and both quantitative and qualitative political-research methods -- rather than deepening any one of those strands at the expense of the others.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum is dominated by a broad political-science core (5 of 24: Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict) together with a law/governance cluster reproducing the programme's international-institutions and EU content (4 of 24: Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Public International Law, Comparative Constitutional Law, Foundations of European Union Law), a full economics cluster reproducing the programme's global-political-economy content (5 of 24: Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior, Public Economics, Econometrics), a quantitative and qualitative methods cluster (2 of 24: Research Methods & Statistics, Qualitative Research Methodology), a history cluster studying the historical and cultural causes of political change (3 of 24: Modern History, History of Empires, Western Way of War), one applied academic-skills/human-rights strand (2 of 24: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy plus one further law course already counted above), a sociology/communication strand implementing governance-of-social-problems and debate/writing skills (3 of 24: Introduction to Sociology, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Persuasive Communication) and Personal & Professional Development. The label names Global Politics because the curriculum reproduces, across political science, law, economics, history and methods, the same breadth of compulsory subject matter -- power, governance, security, comparative regimes, political economy and quantitative/qualitative methods -- that VU's own Global Politics track requires of every student, without foregrounding any single one of those strands as the whole programme.

alternatives.concept: A genuinely different second UCR route evidenced by the two generator-eligible programme-interest rows specifically naming global governance and international institutions (row 5140) and international security (row 5143), supported by target-specific curricular-topic evidence on survey design, big-data analysis and statistics for political science (rows 5150-5152): a concentration studying how conflict, organised crime and radicalisation threaten the global political order, and how international and transnational law, human rights, and quantitative/qualitative data analysis are used to govern and secure it. It replaces the closest match's domestic-comparative-institutional and general-economics/rhetoric breadth with international/transnational law (criminal law, EU law, comparative constitutional law), an applied historical-security research seminar, political psychology of extremism, and data science/machine learning for large-scale political and security data. It honestly preserves that UCR does not offer the programme's own named Global Governance, International Security or Research Project Global Politics units.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum is dominated by an international/transnational law cluster (5 of 24: Law Society & Justice, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy, Introduction to Public International Law, Comparative Constitutional Law, Foundations of European Union Law, plus Criminal Law & Criminal Justice -- 6 of 24 in total) studying the legal architecture of global governance and security, a political-science core (4 of 24: Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, European Union Politics) and its security anchor Peace & Conflict, a history cluster including an applied security-relevant research seminar (4 of 24: Modern History, History of Empires, Western Way of War, History Research Seminar), a data-driven quantitative/qualitative methods cluster (5 of 24: Research Methods & Statistics, Econometrics, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Qualitative Research Methodology), one applied political-psychology course on radicalisation (Youth Resilience to Extremism), a foundational economics pairing (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics) and Personal & Professional Development. The label names International Security, Law and Global Governance because international/transnational law, security studies and data-driven/qualitative research methods -- rather than the closest match's full breadth-replication of the comparator's economics, sociology and communication strands -- are what this curriculum studies in genuine depth.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: VU's own Global Politics track requires every student to take the same compulsory breadth across political science, law, economics, methods and history; the closest match reproduces that generalist breadth in full. This alternative instead deepens one coherent part of that same evidenced field -- international/transnational law, security and data-driven governance analysis -- rather than cosmetically relabelling the closest match. It replaces the closest match's Microeconomics & Behavior, Public Economics, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Persuasive Communication and Introduction to Sociology (5 of 24 courses, 37.5 EC) with Criminal Law & Criminal Justice, History Research Seminar, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning and Youth Resilience to Extremism (5 of 24 courses, 37.5 EC). This is a material curricular consequence, not cosmetic reshuffling: it changes the alternative's academic priorities from breadth-replication of the comparator's full compulsory curriculum to a law-and-data-grounded security/governance concentration, and the two alternatives share 19 of 24 courses while differing in 5 of 24 each way (37.5 EC), well above the pairwise 30-EC/4-course minimum.

progressionAssessment.rationale: No UCR course in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite except the courses that require GOSGATE102 (GOSLAWJ212, GOSLAWJ213, GOSLAWJ312) and BENGATE102 (BENECON211, BENECON212, BENECON312, BENECON311); GOSGATE102 is scheduled in semester 1 and BENGATE102 in semester 2, each before every course that depends on it. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 2, within Year 1. Introductory Year-1 courses (Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Political Philosophy, Foundations of Comparative Politics, Introduction to Economics) are concentrated in semester 1, and level-3 advanced work (Public Economics, Comparative Constitutional Law's prerequisite chain, European Union Politics, Persuasive Communication, Econometrics, Peace & Conflict, Foundations of European Union Law) is concentrated in semesters 4-6, so foundational training precedes advanced work. Where an advisory continuation exists in the course evidence, it is honoured: Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes the more advanced Econometrics (semester 6); The Art of Rhetorical Communication (semester 3) precedes the more advanced Persuasive Communication (semester 5); and Theory of International Relations (semester 2) precedes the more advanced European Union Politics (semester 5) and Peace & Conflict (semester 6). Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest match directly owns thirteen generator-eligible rows: power and international conflict and cooperation (5137, 5138, 5139); the EU's role in the global order (5141); global political economy (5142); comparative politics and political regimes (5144); public administration and the governance of social problems (5145); political theory and the history of political thought (5146); cultural and technological causes of political change (5147); quantitative and qualitative political research (5148, 5149); and writing, debating and presenting political arguments (5153, 5154). The remaining two generator-eligible rows -- global governance and international institutions (5140) and international security (5143) -- were independently assessed as one coherent candidate direction, 'International Security, Law and Global Governance', supported by target-specific curricular-topic evidence on survey design, big-data analysis and statistics (5150-5152). This candidate passes all four gates: it is evidence-backed by two generator-eligible rows naming exactly this territory plus target-specific curricular support; it has a clear organising logic (a law-and-data-grounded security/governance concentration rather than the closest match's breadth-replication of the comparator's full compulsory curriculum); it is substantively distinct, replacing 5 of 24 courses (37.5 EC) with international and transnational law, an applied security-history research seminar, data science/machine learning and political psychology of extremism, materially changing the alternative's academic priorities; and it is mechanically feasible against the enriched course database, with 5 distinct courses (37.5 EC) each way against the closest match, above the pairwise 30-EC/4-course floor. Production therefore includes it as the second alternative. A third candidate, 'Global Political Economy and EU Integration', was then assessed and rejected as not-substantively-distinct: its evidence (rows 5141, EU in world politics, and 5142, global political economy) is already fully owned and instantiated by the closest match, which already schedules UCR's entire relevant Economics catalogue (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior, Public Economics, Econometrics) together with European Union Politics and Foundations of European Union Law; a third alternative built around this evidence would necessarily reuse nearly all of those same courses from both already-included alternatives, leaving no genuinely different 24-course curriculum to build without importing unrelated departments merely to force numerical distinctness or making arbitrary course substitutions that are not genuine consequences of an evidenced concept. Because its own evidence is already substantively covered by the closest match and no genuinely different curriculum follows from it given UCR's actual course offerings, it is rejected as not-substantively-distinct rather than manufactured through arbitrary substitution, and production stops at two included alternatives.

notes.text: Political Science: Global Politics combines ten dedicated compulsory political-science, international-relations and public-administration courses across three years -- comparative politics, IR theory, global governance, the EU in the global order, global political economy, international security, political theory and two full political-science research-project sequences -- taught within a single dedicated Political Science major. At UCR, students can study comparable subject matter, but only through a much smaller dedicated Political Science catalogue (five courses) supplemented by adjacent Law, Economics, History, Sociology and Communication coursework, rather than a single integrated political-science major sequence with its own dedicated research-project courses.
